standard.title: Atomic Model and Radioactive Decay
standard.description: explain how the model of the atom changed following the discovery of electrons, protons and neutrons and describe how natural radioactive decay results in stable atoms
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use particle theory to explain physical properties of substances (AC9S7U05) and classify matter as elements, compounds and mixtures using symbols and formulas (AC9S8U06). They have a functional particle model but it is the simple undifferentiated particle model — particles have no internal structure. They have not yet encountered subatomic particles, the historical development of atomic models, or the concept of nuclear instability and radioactive decay.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how experimental evidence drove the development of the nuclear model of the atom through the discovery of electrons, protons and neutrons, and describe how unstable isotopes undergo radioactive decay (alpha, beta, gamma) to produce stable atoms — including half-life as a measure of decay rate.

nodes.label: The nuclear model of the atom — protons, neutrons and electrons
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the structure of the nuclear atom in terms of protons, neutrons and electrons, and use atomic number and mass number to describe specific atoms.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the nucleus as containing protons and neutrons, with electrons surrounding it, and use atomic number to identify an element.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the relative mass and charge of protons, neutrons and electrons; explain that atomic number equals proton number and determines the element's identity; explain that mass number equals protons plus neutrons; describe electrons as occupying shells around the nucleus; connect to the prior undifferentiated particle model as a simplification that is now being replaced.
wider: Compare the mass and charge of subatomic particles quantitatively — what does the near-zero mass of the electron reveal about where most atomic mass is located?
Examine how the discovery of the nucleus changed scientific understanding — what did Rutherford's gold foil experiment show that Thomson's plum pudding model could not explain?
nodes.hinge_reason: The nuclear model is the structural foundation all subsequent nodes require. Students who cannot correctly assign protons, neutrons and electrons to an atom from its atomic and mass numbers cannot define isotopes in N2, understand why some isotopes are unstable in N3, or follow decay sequences in N4.

response_modes.reason: Students enter with a functional but structure-free particle model. Introducing internal atomic structure requires the prior model to be explicitly extended — particles now have constituent parts. The historical transition from Thomson to Rutherford's model is the elaboration's evidence-based framing for this conceptual shift.

success_criteria: Describes the nuclear atom: protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons in shells
Uses atomic number and mass number to determine proton, neutron and electron counts
Describes the relative mass and charge of protons, neutrons and electrons

nodes.label: Isotopes — same element, different neutron numbers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can define isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, and explain why some isotopes are unstable.
nodes.minimum_width: Students define isotopes correctly and identify that unstable isotopes undergo radioactive decay.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe naturally occurring isotopes of common elements (carbon-12/13/14, uranium-235/238); explain that isotopes have the same chemical properties (same proton number) but different masses; explain that neutron-to-proton ratio affects nuclear stability; describe unstable isotopes as those with configurations that tend toward decay; connect carbon-14 specifically to radiocarbon dating.
wider: Investigate how radiocarbon dating has been used to establish that First Peoples of Australia have been present for more than 60,000 years — what does the carbon-14 decay rate reveal about sample age?
Compare stable and unstable isotope distributions for a named element and identify what neutron-to-proton ratios characterise stability

response_modes.reason: Isotopes require students to understand that atomic identity is determined by proton number alone — same protons, different neutrons, same element. This is the prerequisite for understanding why only some atoms decay (unstable neutron-to-proton ratios) in N3.

success_criteria: Defines isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Identifies that some isotopes are unstable and undergo radioactive decay

nodes.label: Types of radioactive decay — alpha, beta and gamma
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe alpha, beta and gamma decay in terms of what is emitted and how each changes the nucleus, and compare their penetrating power.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe what is emitted in each decay type (alpha particle, beta particle, gamma ray) and state one difference in their penetrating power.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe alpha decay as emission of a helium nucleus (reducing atomic number by 2, mass number by 4); describe beta decay as emission of an electron from the nucleus (increasing atomic number by 1); describe gamma emission as release of high-energy electromagnetic radiation with no change to atomic number or mass; compare penetrating power (alpha — stopped by paper, beta — by aluminium, gamma — reduced by lead/concrete); describe applications in medicine and industry.
wider: Investigate the use of radioactive isotopes in medicine — how is the type of decay and half-life matched to the diagnostic or treatment application?
Examine how gamma radiation is used to check for faults in aircraft and spacecraft materials — what property of gamma makes it suitable for this application?
nodes.hinge_reason: The three decay types are the mechanistic content of the descriptor's 'describe how natural radioactive decay results in stable atoms' demand. Students who cannot distinguish decay types — particularly students who conflate alpha/beta emission with gamma, or who cannot track changes to atomic and mass numbers — cannot follow decay sequences toward stability in N4 or understand why different isotopes have different applications.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Medical and industrial applications of radioactive isotopes are explicitly named in the elaborations and provide genuine investigative width. Each application requires matching decay type and half-life to context — a richer application of the decay model than identification alone.

response_modes.reason: Alpha, beta and gamma are qualitatively different in emission type, effect on nucleus, and penetrating power. Students need a clear comparison framework — what is emitted, what changes in the nucleus, how far it penetrates — before applying decay to stability sequences.

Medical imaging, cancer treatment, materials testing, and radiocarbon dating are each a distinct application context that requires matching decay type to purpose. These contexts build genuine understanding of why decay type matters beyond identification.

success_criteria: Describes what is emitted in alpha, beta and gamma decay
Explains how alpha and beta decay change the atomic number and mass number of the nucleus
Compares the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation

nodes.label: Half-life — rate of radioactive decay
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can define half-life, use half-life data to calculate remaining activity after a given number of half-lives, and explain how half-life determines the suitability of isotopes for different applications.
nodes.minimum_width: Students define half-life as the time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay and calculate remaining quantity after two half-lives.
nodes.typical_width: Students apply half-life calculations across multiple timescales (carbon-14 at 5,730 years, uranium-238 at 4.5 billion years); interpret decay curves graphically; explain why short-lived isotopes are suitable for medical imaging and long-lived ones for geological dating; explain that half-life is constant and unaffected by physical or chemical conditions.
wider: Simulate radioactive decay using digital tools or physical models (dice) and compare the simulated decay curve to the mathematical model
Investigate how uranium-238 half-life data is used in geological dating — what assumptions must be true for radiometric dating to give accurate ages?

response_modes.reason: Half-life is a probabilistic concept — it describes the behaviour of large populations of nuclei, not individual atoms. Students commonly expect individual atoms to decay at half-life intervals. Making the probabilistic nature explicit, and connecting the constant half-life to practical application matching, completes the decay model.

success_criteria: Defines half-life as the time for half of the nuclei in a sample to decay
Calculates the remaining quantity of a radioisotope after a given number of half-lives
Explains why half-life determines the suitability of an isotope for a named application

nodes.label: Decay sequences — how unstable isotopes reach stability
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how a series of decay events transforms an unstable isotope into a stable one, and explain the relationship between the descriptor's descriptor claim that 'natural radioactive decay results in stable atoms'.
nodes.minimum_width: Students trace a simple one or two-step decay sequence (e.g. radon-222 → polonium-218 via alpha decay) and identify the stable end product.
nodes.typical_width: Students trace multi-step decay chains (e.g. uranium-238 → lead-206); track changes to atomic number and mass number at each step; explain that each decay step moves the nucleus toward a more stable neutron-to-proton ratio; connect to the historical development of atomic theory — decay provided early evidence for nuclear structure.
wider: Investigate how mass and energy are connected in nuclear reactions — what happens to the 'missing mass' in a decay event? (binding energy / E=mc² at a qualitative level)
Examine how the discovery of radioactive decay changed the understanding of the atom's internal structure — what did natural transmutation reveal that the earlier model could not explain?

response_modes.reason: This node brings together the nuclear model (N1), isotope instability (N2), decay types (N3) and half-life (N4) into a complete account of how decay sequences produce stable atoms — the descriptor's explicit endpoint. Tracing a decay chain exercises all prior nodes in sequence.

success_criteria: Traces a named decay sequence and identifies the stable end product
Tracks changes to atomic number and mass number at each decay step
Explains how the sequence of decay events moves the nucleus toward stability
